subsystems.name: Hardness assumptions
subsystems.role: the mathematical problems whose difficulty is the whole basis of security.
parts: parameter sets sized against the best known lattice-reduction attacks

subsystems.name: Polynomial arithmetic engine
subsystems.role: fast multiplication and reduction of long polynomials over a large finite field.

subsystems.name: Key and ciphertext logic
subsystems.role: the actual key establishment and signature operations built on that arithmetic.

subsystems.name: Randomness and sampling
subsystems.role: turns random bytes into the structured small errors the schemes need.

subsystems.name: Encoding and serialisation
subsystems.role: packing keys and ciphertexts into fixed byte strings that fit existing protocols.

subsystems.name: Side-channel hardening
subsystems.role: stops an attacker reading secrets from timing, power draw or a single injected fault.
parts: re-encryption and consistency checks in decapsulation

buildSteps.title: Pick the problem and parameters
buildSteps.detail: Choose a lattice problem — module-LWE or NTRU-style — then set ring dimension and modulus so both classical and quantum attack estimates land far above the required security level, without making keys unusably large.

buildSteps.title: Write the ring arithmetic
buildSteps.detail: Implement multiplication of polynomials of degree a few hundred in a ring modulus a prime, using a number-theoretic transform so the cost is close to n log n rather than n squared.

buildSteps.title: Sample the errors
buildSteps.detail: Generate secret and error polynomials from a tight, carefully specified distribution — a wider or narrower distribution than specified weakens or breaks the scheme.

buildSteps.title: Build key exchange and signatures
buildSteps.detail: Assemble key generation, encapsulation and decapsulation for the KEM; separately build the rejection-sampling loop that lattice signatures need, which must not leak through timing.

buildSteps.title: Encode and interop-test
buildSteps.detail: Serialise keys and ciphertexts to exact byte lengths, fix them into certificate and handshake structures, and check against published known-answer test vectors.

buildSteps.title: Harden the implementation
buildSteps.detail: Convert all secret-dependent code paths to constant time, mask arithmetic against power analysis, and add checks that catch a fault-injected ciphertext before it is decapsulated.

buildSteps.title: Validate
buildSteps.detail: Run test vectors, independent implementations, formal verification where available, and side-channel evaluation on real hardware before any deployment.

buildSteps.title: Integrate into protocols
buildSteps.detail: Add the scheme to TLS 1.3, IKEv2, SSH and certificate tooling, initially alongside classical elliptic-curve key exchange in a hybrid so security holds if either is broken.

buildSteps.title: Deploy with crypto-agility
buildSteps.detail: Roll out hybrids, keep the ability to swap algorithms quickly, and retain classical algorithms in parallel until post-quantum schemes have survived years of public cryptanalysis.

prerequisites.tech: Quantum computers able to run Shor's algorithm at cryptographic scale
prerequisites.why: it is the threat that motivates all of this; today's machines factor only tiny numbers, but a future one would break RSA and elliptic-curve key exchange.
these reductions are what let a scheme's security rest on hard lattice problems rather than on unproven guesswork.

prerequisites.tech: Efficient modular arithmetic and transform libraries
prerequisites.why: lattice schemes are only practical because fast polynomial multiplication over finite fields is a solved problem.
sampling errors and generating secrets fails catastrophically with weak randomness.
lattice schemes are more exposed to timing and fault attacks than the elliptic curves they replace, and not all processors or HSMs help avoid that.
schemes are useless until browsers, servers, certificate authorities and hardware tokens carry them end to end.

pathway.milestone: finalised standards for lattice key encapsulation and signatures, with hybrid key exchange already running in browsers, messaging apps and TLS test deployments
pathway.unlocks: real-world data on performance, interoperability and attack surface.

pathway.milestone: hardware and firmware support — HSMs, secure elements, smart cards and low-power devices
pathway.unlocks: post-quantum security for payments, identity documents and anything without a fast general-purpose CPU.

pathway.milestone: retirement of classic RSA and elliptic-curve key transport where hybrid is already proven
pathway.unlocks: protection against 'harvest now, decrypt later' collection of today's traffic.

pathway.milestone: signature migration and periodic parameter review as cryptanalysis matures
pathway.unlocks: a stable post-quantum public-key infrastructure that can absorb the next algorithmic break without another decade-long rebuild.
